extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, judges, and litigants (those evaluating §101 patent-eligibility of inventions, especially computer-implemented claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal framework and standards for determining whether patent claims (particularly computer-implemented/business-method claims) are eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, using the Mayo two-step framework and precedent (Benson, Flook, Bilski, Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit §101 exception: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: We have long held that this provision contains an important implicit exception: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds the §101 inquiry; such items are ‘the basic tools of scientific and technological work,’ and monopolization of them through patents risks impeding innovation. Use this exception as the starting point for determining eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo two-step framework for evaluating §101
rubrics_metrics.description: First, determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). If so, then consider the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second step is a search for an 'inventive concept'—an element or combination sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify 'abstract idea' broadly (includes fundamental economic practices and organizational methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas include methods of organizing human activity and fundamental economic practices long prevalent in commerce (e.g., hedging in Bilski; intermediated settlement in Alice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confine 'abstract ideas' to mathematical formulas or natural truths; longstanding commercial practices and methods of organizing human activity can be abstract and fall outside §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere recitation of generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality, to a method already well known in the art is not enough to supply the 'inventive concept' needed to make the transformation. Stating an abstract idea while adding the words 'apply it with a computer' simply combines those two steps, with the same deficient result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim only instructs implementation of an abstract idea on an unspecified, generic computer, that does not provide 'practical assurance' that the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the idea. Compare with Benson and Flook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an 'inventive concept' beyond conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites an abstract idea must include 'additional features' that supply an inventive concept sufficient to transform the claimed abstract idea into a patent-eligible application; simply applying well-understood, routine, conventional activities is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claimed elements are well-known and routine (e.g., electronic recordkeeping, obtaining data, adjusting balances, issuing instructions). If they are conventional, they do not constitute an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine if additional elements transform the claim, courts must consider the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to see if the combination adds something not present when steps are considered separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual elements are ordinary, an innovative ordered combination that changes the nature or improves technology may supply the inventive concept (contrast Diehr where combination improved a technological process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility when claim improves computer functioning or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are patent eligible when they use an abstract idea in a manner that improves an existing technological process or the functioning of the computer itself (Diehr: use of a mathematical equation within a process that solved a technological problem transformed the claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concrete technical improvements (new ways of measuring, controlling, or interfacing with hardware; novel algorithms tied to specific computer architecture) rather than mere use of a computer to perform abstract steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: System and media claims must recite meaningful hardware limitations beyond generic components
rubrics_metrics.description: System claims that merely recite a handful of generic computer components (e.g., data processing system, communications controller, data storage unit) configured to implement the abstract idea add nothing of substance and are not patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language describing generic hardware that performs routine calculation, storage, and transmission functions does not avoid §101 ineligibility; avoid allowing patent eligibility to 'depend simply on the draftsman's art.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-emption concern as a guide to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: A key concern underlying the §101 exception is pre-emption: patents that would pre-empt use of basic tools or grant a monopoly over abstract ideas risk impeding innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim would effectively pre-empt use of the abstract idea across fields; if so, that argues for ineligibility. This is a policy rationale informing the substantive test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precedent examples as touchstones for ineligible/eligible claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior cases identify illustrative examples: Benson (algorithm converting BCD to binary — abstract), Flook (mathematical formula for alarm limits — abstract), Bilski (hedging — abstract), Diehr (computer-implemented rubber-curing process — eligible because it improved a technological process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed invention to these precedents to determine whether it more closely resembles an abstract idea merely implemented on a computer or a technological improvement that transforms the claim into eligible subject matter.
